'''mmWave sensing''' is a [[remote sensing]] technique using [[Extremely high frequency|millimeter wave]] (mmWave) [[radar]] to measure displacement as small as a fraction of a millimeter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=mmWave radar sensors {{!}} TI.com |url=https://www.ti.com/sensors/mmwave-radar/overview.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=www.ti.com |language=en-US}}</ref> This system requires a mmWave radar sensor to transmit and receive pulses of millimeter electromagnetic wave energy, detecting targets and motion from the reflections it receives back.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MmWave Radar Applications and Advantages |url=https://resources.system-analysis.cadence.com/blog/msa2022-mmwave-radar-applications-and-advantages |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=resources.system-analysis.cadence.com |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Additional components such as converters, [[Signal processing|signal processors]] and other embedded technologies create new use cases and improve performance of the system.<ref>{{Cite web |title=mmWave radar sensors {{!}} TI.com |url=https://www.ti.com/sensors/mmwave-radar/overview.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=www.ti.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Current applications for this technology include human and animal movement tracking, [[human presence detection]], and detection of [[vital signs]] for use across automotive, meteorological, medical and pet health industries and is often an alternative to wearable-based technologies for the same uses.<ref>{{Cite book |date=2016 |doi=10.1109/IPSN.2016.7460704 |s2cid=14106463 |language=en-US |last1=Zeng |first1=Yunze |last2=Pathak |first2=Parth H. |last3=Yang |first3=Zhicheng |last4=Mohapatra |first4=Prasant |title=2016 15th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Information Processing in Sensor Networks (IPSN) |chapter=Poster Abstract: Human Tracking and Activity Monitoring Using 60 GHZ mmWave |pages=1–2 |isbn=978-1-5090-0802-5 }}</ref>

==Background==
Compared to sensing technologies using other [[Radio frequency|radio frequencies]] in the [[electromagnetic spectrum]] such as [[infrared]] or [[ultra-wideband]], mmWave uses 30 to 300 gigahertz (GHz). Typical mmWave sensors use the 24-, 60- and 77-GHz band each with their own benefits for specific applications.<ref>{{Cite book |date=2021 |doi=10.1109/ISAPE54070.2021.9753337 |s2cid=248249335 |language=en-US |last1=Liu |first1=Hanling |last2=Miao |first2=Miao |last3=Huang |first3=Suying |last4=Luo |first4=Yunlong |last5=Qi |first5=Alex |last6=Qi |first6=Yihong |last7=Ma |first7=Jianhua |title=2021 13th International Symposium on Antennas, Propagation and EM Theory (ISAPE) |chapter=A Perspective on Pet Emotion Monitoring Using Millimeter Wave Radar |pages=1–3 |isbn=978-1-6654-1812-6 }} 
</ref>

==Applications==
===Automotive===
mmWave sensing can be used inside vehicles to improve driver and passenger safety and comfort functions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-04-30 |title=Detecting vehicle occupancy with mmWave sensors - Automotive - Technical articles - TI E2E support forums |url=https://e2e.ti.com/blogs_/b/behind_the_wheel/posts/detecting-vehicle-occupancy-with-mmwave-sensors |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=e2e.ti.com |language=en}}</ref> Notable advantages of using mmWave technology in vehicles revolve around its capability to operate effectively in spaces with low-lighting and limited visibility. mmWave sensing can penetrate materials like plastic, textiles, and glass, making it contactless.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-04-30 |title=Detecting vehicle occupancy with mmWave sensors - Automotive - Technical articles - TI E2E support forums |url=https://e2e.ti.com/blogs_/b/behind_the_wheel/posts/detecting-vehicle-occupancy-with-mmwave-sensors |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=e2e.ti.com |language=en}}</ref>

Recent applications for automotive mmWave sensing include:
*Occupancy detection
*Child presence detection (CPD) <ref>{{Cite web |last=AG |first=Infineon Technologies |title=60 GHz Radar Sensor for Occupant Monitoring (OMS) - Infineon Technologies |url=https://www.infineon.com/cms/en/applications/automotive/chassis-safety-and-adas/in-cabin-sensing/occupant-monitoring-system-oms/ |access-date=2024-05-10 |website=www.infineon.com |language=en}}</ref>
*Seatbelt reminders
*Optimized airbag deployment
*Monitoring of driver vital signs<ref>{{Cite web |title=Millimeter Wave Radar System Keeps Drivers Safe on the Road - IEEE Spectrum |url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/millimeter-wave-radar-system-cars |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=[[IEEE]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Assisted Living and Elderly Care===
mmWave sensing can be used in homes and [[nursing home]]s to assist seniors, individuals [[aging in place]], and caregivers. Using mmWave technology is non-intrusive as it does not use cameras or microphones for its applications, and does not require patients to use [[Wearable technology|wearable devices]] for tracking.

Use-cases in assisted living and elderly care include:
*Fall detection
*Posture detection
*Occupancy detection
*Vital signs monitoring<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Iyer |first1=Srikrishna |last2=Zhao |first2=Leo |last3=Mohan |first3=Manoj Prabhakar |last4=Jimeno |first4=Joe |last5=Siyal |first5=Mohammed Yakoob |last6=Alphones |first6=Arokiaswami |last7=Karim |first7=Muhammad Faeyz |date=2022-04-19 |title=mm-Wave Radar-Based Vital Signs Monitoring and Arrhythmia Detection Using Machine Learning |journal=Sensors (Basel, Switzerland) |volume=22 |issue=9 |pages=3106 |doi=10.3390/s22093106 |issn=1424-8220 |pmc=9104941 |pmid=35590796 |bibcode=2022Senso..22.3106I |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Smart Home===
Integrated within applications for presence and occupancy detection, mmWave sensing can be applied to the smart home to enable home automations without requiring wearable technology or cameras.
Applications include:
*Water level detection of toilets<ref>{{Cite book |date=2021 |doi=10.1109/ISAPE54070.2021.9752979 |s2cid=248258584 |language=en-US |last1=Yang |first1=Yang |last2=Chi |first2=Lidong |last3=Luo |first3=Yunlong |last4=Qi |first4=Alex |last5=Miao |first5=Miao |last6=Qi |first6=Yihong |title=2021 13th International Symposium on Antennas, Propagation and EM Theory (ISAPE) |chapter=Antenna Design of Millimeter Wave Radar for Smart Toilet |pages=1–3 |isbn=978-1-6654-1812-6 }}</ref>
*Sleep apnea tracking <ref>{{Cite book |date=2022 |doi=10.1109/BIBE55377.2022.00065 |s2cid=254640679 |language=en-US |last1=Chen |first1=Fu-Kuei |last2=Wang |first2=You-Kwang |last3=Lin |first3=Hsin-Piao |last4=Chen |first4=Chien-Yu |last5=Yeh |first5=Shu-Ming |last6=Wang |first6=Ching-Yu |title=2022 IEEE 22nd International Conference on Bioinformatics and Bioengineering (BIBE) |chapter=Feasibility Study for Apnea Screening in Patients' Homes Using Radar and Machine Learning Method |pages=282–287 |isbn=978-1-6654-8487-9 }}</ref>
*Smart lighting control <ref>{{Cite web |title=Radar vs. PIR for lighting control |url=https://www.novelic.com/blog/the-advantages-of-mmwave-radar-sensors-over-pir-sensors-for-lighting-control-and-smart-lighting-applications/ |access-date=2024-05-10 |website=NOVELIC |language=en}}</ref>

===Other===
Other applications for mmWave sensing include pet monitoring, where the technology can be used to track and monitor animal vital signs to interpret pet emotions.<ref>{{Cite book |date=2021 |doi=10.1109/ISAPE54070.2021.9753337 |s2cid=248249335 |language=en-US |last1=Liu |first1=Hanling |last2=Miao |first2=Miao |last3=Huang |first3=Suying |last4=Luo |first4=Yunlong |last5=Qi |first5=Alex |last6=Qi |first6=Yihong |last7=Ma |first7=Jianhua |title=2021 13th International Symposium on Antennas, Propagation and EM Theory (ISAPE) |chapter=A Perspective on Pet Emotion Monitoring Using Millimeter Wave Radar |pages=1–3 |isbn=978-1-6654-1812-6 }}</ref>
